name: Optimising Lab Protocols
title: Optimising Lab Protocols
answer: Optimising lab protocols covers the use of AI and simulation to improve experimental procedures in laboratory settings, including reagent volumes, timing, temperature, and the order of steps. It spans wet lab biology, chemistry, and analytical workflows where small changes can affect yield, reproducibility, and cost. The aim is to find protocols that are more robust, faster, or cheaper without running every possible combination by hand. This work sits within laboratory automation and simulation, drawing on the site's library of research papers and extracted claims.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work typically runs on standard laboratory information management systems, robotic liquid handlers, and scheduling software connected to simulation engines. Models may be trained on historical protocol logs, instrument telemetry, and published experimental data. Cloud or on-premises compute is used for Bayesian optimisation and digital twin simulations, often integrated with electronic lab notebooks. The site's catalogue of 801 scientific models includes many relevant to protocol simulation and outcome prediction.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A protocol is represented as a sequence of actions with parameters, and a surrogate model predicts outcomes such as yield, purity, or cycle time. Design of experiments, Bayesian optimisation, and reinforcement learning are common approaches for proposing new parameter sets. These proposals are tested in simulation or on automated hardware, and the results feed back to update the model. Active learning reduces the number of physical experiments needed by focusing on the most informative conditions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance of training data and simulation assumptions must be recorded so that a recommended protocol can be traced to its source papers and instrument logs. Risks include overfitting to a specific machine or reagent lot, and unsafe parameter combinations if constraints are not encoded. Rights in protocol data may belong to the lab or institution, and published protocols carry licenses that affect reuse. Changes to lab protocols can also affect safety, waste, and regulatory compliance, so human review remains part of the workflow.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward closed-loop systems where robotic labs propose, run, and refine protocols with minimal human intervention. Self-driving laboratories and foundation models for experimental design are emerging, but human oversight remains necessary for safety and interpretation. The site's extracted claims and model catalogue will support more systematic comparison of optimisation methods across different experimental domains.
